c.tagline: The Gambia's buzzing heart — markets, beaches, and the Senegambia strip.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow town taxis and shared 'gelly-gelly' minibuses run fixed local routes for a few dalasi; green 'tourist taxis' are unmetered—always agree the fare before getting in. There are no ride-hailing apps.

emergency.note: 117 police, 116 ambulance, 118 fire. Response can be slow—hotels usually arrange private transport for emergencies.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Petty crime and “bumster” touts on the tourist beaches; caution at night

hood_desc: The Gambia's tourism epicentre, where the Senegambia Strip packs restaurants, bars, live-music venues, casinos, and craft markets along a short road behind a long sandy beach lined with resort hotels; the go-to base for nightlife and dining.
A relaxed beach-resort area just north, known for its long strand, hotels, a golf course, and the birdwatching hotspot of Kotu Creek; easygoing and good for families and nature lovers.

An older coastal town with real Gambian character, home to the Kachikally Crocodile Pool, the botanical gardens, Cape Point beaches, and a busy fish market; blends sightseeing with everyday local life.
A leafy, upscale district of diplomatic residences, embassies, the golf club, and some of the coast's better restaurants; calm, green, and residential, close to the beach without the strip's crowds.

The bustling commercial core around Sayerr Jobe Avenue and the country's largest market—a chaotic, colourful sprawl of stalls selling everything from batik and produce to electronics; authentic and inexpensive but far from the tourist polish.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only.

transit.hours: Public buses and gelly-gelly minibuses run from early morning until early evening; after dark you rely on taxis.
transit.note: Serekunda has no rail or tram. Green GTSC public buses and privately run 'gelly-gelly' shared minibuses cover fixed routes, supplemented by yellow town taxis and green tourist taxis.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or apprentice on board (a few dalasi for gelly-gelly and buses); there is no transit card.

transit.m: Shared taxi / gelly-gelly toward Serekunda (~40 min)
Green tourist taxi to the Kombo hotels (25-30 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or leaving about 10% for good service in tourist restaurants is appreciated.

food.name: Benachin
food.desc: Gambia's one-pot rice, ancestor of jollof: rice cooked in tomato, onion and fish or meat stock with cassava, carrot and bitter tomato.

places.name: Paradiso Restaurant
places.note: Long-running local favourite for African plates including benachin and domoda.

places.name: African Queen Restaurant
places.note: Straightforward Gambian cooking at local prices; benachin is a lunchtime staple.

places.name: Serekunda Market food stalls
places.note: Women cook benachin in huge pots at midday; cheapest and most authentic version in town.

food.name: Domoda
food.desc: The national dish: a thick groundnut stew of beef, chicken or fish slow-cooked with tomato and pumpkin, ladled over white rice.

places.name: Paradiso Restaurant
places.note: Known for traditional domoda and yassa served in generous portions.

places.name: Scala Restaurant
places.note: Where local and international menus meet; a comfortable sit-down place to try domoda.

places.name: Serekunda Market food stalls
places.note: Lunch-only stalls dishing domoda straight from the pot for a couple of dalasi.

food.name: Yassa
food.desc: Chicken or fish marinated in lemon, mustard and onion, then grilled and simmered back into a tangy onion sauce. Served with rice.

places.name: Paradiso Restaurant
places.note: Reliably good yassa poulet, one of the dishes the restaurant is best known for.

places.name: The Clay Oven
places.note: Popular local restaurant blending Gambian and Indian cooking; yassa on the African side.

places.name: Sea Shells Bar and Restaurant
places.note: Casual spot for yassa fish using the day's catch from the coast.

food.name: Afra
food.desc: Gambian late-night barbecue: lamb, goat or beef grilled over charcoal, chopped on the block with onion, mustard and chilli, wrapped in tapalapa bread.

places.name: Westfield Junction afra grills
places.note: Cluster of charcoal grills that fire up after dark; the classic Serekunda afra stop.

places.name: Kairaba Avenue afra stalls
places.note: Roadside grills running late along the main avenue; point at the cut you want.

places.name: Serekunda Market surrounds
places.note: Evening grills around the market edge, busiest and freshest after sunset.

food.name: Superkanja
food.desc: Rich okra stew cooked down with palm oil, smoked fish, beef or lamb and plenty of chilli, eaten over rice. Thick, glossy and deeply savoury.

places.name: African Queen Restaurant
places.note: Home-style Gambian menu that rotates superkanja and plasas through the week.

places.name: Serekunda Market food stalls
places.note: Best chance of finding superkanja, since it is a household dish more than a menu dish.

places.name: Scala Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down option where you can ask for the day's Gambian stew of the moment.

food.name: Akara and Tapalapa
food.desc: Breakfast on the street: black-eyed pea fritters fried to order and stuffed into a length of crusty tapalapa bread with hot pepper sauce.

places.name: Serekunda Market
places.note: Fritter pans go from first light; buy the bread from the baker two stalls along.

places.name: Westfield Junction street vendors
places.note: Morning carts selling akara, ebbeh and bean sandwiches to the commuter crowd.

places.name: Latrikunda market stalls
places.note: Neighbourhood market with the same breakfast line-up and almost no tourists.

food.name: Wonjo and Bouye
food.desc: The two homemade non-alcoholic staples: wonjo, a deep-red hibiscus infusion, and bouye, creamy baobab-fruit juice with vanilla. Both served ice cold.

places.name: Serekunda Market drink sellers
places.note: Sold in frozen plastic pouches or bottles; look for the sellers with cool boxes.

places.name: Paradiso Restaurant
places.note: Bottled wonjo and baobab juice served with meals, a safer bet on hygiene.

places.name: Westfield Junction juice stalls
places.note: Busy corner stands with high turnover, so the juice is made fresh daily.

food.name: Attaya
food.desc: Gunpowder green tea brewed strong with lots of sugar and poured from height into foaming shot glasses, over three rounds. A social ritual, not a quick drink.

places.name: Serekunda street-corner attaya circles
places.note: Small charcoal burners on every street; being invited to join is normal and expected.

places.name: Serekunda Market tea stalls
places.note: Vendors brew all day beside the stalls; the second round is traditionally the best.

places.name: Westfield Junction
places.note: Plenty of attaya set-ups around the transport hub while you wait for a gelly-gelly.

landmarks: Serekunda Market
The Gambia's largest and liveliest market, a maze of stalls piled with batik fabrics, spices, produce and crafts at the heart of the city.
Kachikally Crocodile Pool
A sacred pool in nearby Bakau where dozens of docile Nile crocodiles bask among pilgrims seeking fertility blessings, with a small ethnographic museum.
Bijilo Forest Park (Monkey Park)
A coastal reserve of gallery forest and dunes where green vervet and red colobus monkeys scamper along shaded walking trails near Kololi.
Senegambia Strip
The buzzing hub of Gambian tourism in Kololi, lined with restaurants, bars and craft stalls, and famous for its evening street life.
Kotu Beach
A broad golden Atlantic beach beside Kotu Creek, beloved for juice-bar sunsets, fishing pirogues and some of West Africa's easiest birdwatching.
Abuko Nature Reserve
The Gambia's first wildlife reserve, a compact pocket of rainforest minutes from town teeming with monkeys, monitor lizards, crocodiles and 250-plus bird species.
Arch 22
Banjul's monumental 35-metre cream-coloured gateway arch, built to mark the 1994 coup, offering museum exhibits and rooftop views over the capital nearby.
Tanji Fish Market
A sensory riot of brightly painted pirogues, smokehouses and fish auctions on the beach at Tanji, the coast's most photogenic working fishing village.
National Museum of The Gambia
Banjul's modest but engaging museum traces Gambian history, music and ethnography, an easy cultural excursion from Serekunda.
Brikama Craft Market
A renowned woodcarving centre south of Serekunda where generations of artisans chisel masks, drums and statues before your eyes.

train.note: The Gambia has no railways at all. The short colonial-era lines around Bathurst (now Banjul), Kuntaur and Kaur were lifted in the 1960s and nothing has replaced them, so every land journey is by road. The nearest passenger rail of any kind is Senegal's Dakar TER commuter line roughly 300 km north, which is of no practical use for reaching Serekunda; the old Dakar - Bamako line no longer carries passengers.

intl.to: Dakar & Ziguinchor (Senegal) - via the Amdalai/Karang or Seleti crossings, with the Trans-Gambia bridge at Farafenni for the northern route
intl.op: sept-place shared taxis and coaches from the Serekunda and Brikama garages — tickets at the garage

bus.note: Serekunda's transport hubs are the garages at Westfield Junction and in the town itself, plus the much bigger Brikama garage about 20 km south which is the departure point for Ziguinchor in the Casamance. The state operator Gambia Transport Service Company (GTSC) runs scheduled coaches from the Banjul-Serekunda area upcountry to Soma, Janjanbureh and Basse Santa Su, an 8-10 hour trip on the south bank road, while shared gelli-gelli minibuses and Senegalese sept-place Peugeot estates cover shorter hops and the border runs. Nothing is sold online - you pay at the garage and the vehicle leaves when it is full. Dakar takes 6-9 hours depending on border queues and whether you use the Farafenni bridge or the Barra ferry.

intl.to: Barra (The Gambia) - from the Banjul ferry terminal about 13 km from Serekunda, 45-60 min across the mouth of the Gambia River, connecting to Karang for Senegal
intl.op: Gambia Ports Authority ferry service — tickets at the terminal

ferry.note: The Banjul - Barra ferry is the main link to the north bank and the usual first leg towards Senegal's Sine-Saloum and Dakar, crossing the river mouth in 45-60 minutes from the terminal at the end of Liberation Avenue in Banjul. It is crowded, frequently delayed and the vessels have a poor reliability record, with vehicles sometimes queuing for hours; there is no advance booking, so foot passengers simply buy at the window and board. Since the Senegambia bridge opened at Farafenni in 2019 most through road traffic bypasses the ferry altogether. Banjul's port otherwise handles cargo only and there are no international passenger sailings.

half.name: Makasutu Culture Forest
half.blurb: A private reserve of mangroves and palm forest along a tidal creek, with canoe trips and cultural performances.

half.name: Bao Bolong Wetland Reserve
half.blurb: A mangrove-lined tributary of the Gambia River near Kartong, explored by boat for birdwatching and crocodile sightings.

full.name: Wassu Stone Circles
full.blurb: A UNESCO-listed complex of laterite stone monuments erected over a thousand years ago, part of a network across the Gambia River basin.

full.name: Janjanbureh
full.blurb: A river island town founded as a British anti-slavery settlement, with colonial ruins and access to River Gambia National Park's chimpanzees.
